title: A man raced the Harwell computer by hand and kept up for about half an hour

cover.alt: Racks of the Harwell Dekatron computer packed with rows of glass tubes, some glowing orange, beside cream-coloured relay cans.

body: The **Harwell Dekatron** computer, built at Britain's Atomic Energy Research Establishment and working from 1951, was slow even for its day: a multiplication took between 5 and 10 seconds, so a skilled human with a desk calculator could match it. What it had was stamina. It was so reliable that from May 1952 to February 1953 it ran for an average of 80 hours a week, and it could be left alone for days with a long punched tape to work through. Restored at The National Museum of Computing between 2009 and 2012, it was recognised by Guinness World Records in 2013 as the world's oldest working digital computer.

slides.text: He kept level for about half an hour working flat out, but had to retire, exhausted; the machine just ploughed on.
slides.attribution: Jack Howlett, on hand-computer Bart Fossey's race with the machine

slides.heading: Rank its parts, most numerous first
slides.explanation: Its memory was 828 dekatrons, glowing tubes that each hold one decimal digit, so you can watch the numbers it stores.

slides.heading: Ten days on its own
slides.text: Jack Howlett, who ran the Harwell computer laboratory, recalled that its record was over one Christmas and New Year holiday. Left alone with miles of punched tape as input, it ran for at least ten days and was still ticking away when the staff came back.

events.text: Won by a Wolverhampton college and renamed WITCH

slides.label: the weight of the whole machine
slides.text: It stands 2 m high and 6 m wide, and by one restorer's reckoning stores 90 numbers in all: roughly a person with a pocket calculator.

slides.question: What made such a slow computer worth building?
options: It could run unattended for days
It was the fastest of its time
It was the first to use transistors
slides.explanation: Its designer wrote that a slow computer only justifies itself if it runs for long periods unattended. People could match its speed, but not for days on end.
